caveats: Randomness is uniform complete randomization of fixed finite populations; sample covariances use the paper’s arm-size divisor, and centered, standardized covariates have population mean zero and population Gram matrix equal to the identity.

The exact unbiasedness results and the estimator expansions highlighted above impose invertibility for every assignment, eventually in the asymptotic results, and do not cover a generalized-inverse extension. Other moment and order bounds use the hypotheses in their individual statements.

The sequence assumptions use one second-moment bound across sample sizes, arms and covariate coordinates, allocation fractions bounded away from zero and one, and eventual covariate standardization; dimension may vary with sample size.

The conditional covariance repair assumes the closed proposition `AronowAudit.Literature.LeiDing2021QuadraticSampling`; the conditional interacted expansion assumes `AronowAudit.Literature.Tropp2011RowSampling`, rather than supplying proofs of those published inputs.
The selected interacted exact decomposition covers the valid part of Theorem 4.1; its printed third-component signs and endpoint expansion are addressed separately in the corrections.

corrections.what: Lemma A.1 prints a covariance-estimator variance bound for arbitrary uncentered vectors; a six-unit population sampled four units at a time has variance $16607/4800$, exceeding the printed bound $3829/1440$.

The uncentered variance bound of Lemma A.1 is replaced by a bound using population-centered vectors on its right-hand side, with the printed expectation formula retained, conditional on Lei and Ding (2021), Supplementary Lemma A.5, as encoded by `LeiDing2021QuadraticSampling`.

The printed third bias component in Theorem 4.1 has the wrong signs: a standardized six-unit population with nonsingular arm fits gives the actual component $217/2500$, while the printed expression gives $-217/2500$.

Reversing both signs in the printed third bias-component formula of Theorem 4.1 yields the exact control-minus-treated expectation identity under complete randomization with centered covariates, $n\ge3$ and nonempty arms.

The printed condition $\kappa_n\log d_n\to0$ does not suffice for the interacted stochastic expansion: an admissible sequence with $d_n=1$, nonsingular fits and $\kappa_n\to1$ satisfies that condition but its remainder is not $O_p(\sqrt{\kappa_n/n})$.

Replacing the printed condition by $\kappa_n\log\max\{d_n,2\}\to0$ gives the interacted residual expansion with remainder $O_p(\sqrt{\kappa_nd_n/n})$ under the sequence assumptions stated in the caveats and eventual armwise nonsingularity for every assignment, conditional on Tropp (2011), Lemma 3.4, as encoded by `Tropp2011RowSampling`.

key_results.what: For $n\ge3$ under complete randomization with nonempty arms, standardized covariates and nonsingular noninteracted fits for every assignment, the proposed bias estimator is unbiased for the adjustment bias and the debiased estimator is unbiased for the finite-population average treatment effect.

Under the analogous finite-sample assumptions with nonsingular fits in both arms for every assignment, the interacted bias estimator estimates the adjustment bias without bias, the debiased treatment contrast is unbiased, and each debiased arm expression is unbiased for its population outcome mean.

For $n\ge3$ with nonempty arms, standardized covariates and nonsingular noninteracted fits under complete randomization, the exact slope and bias decompositions hold, with the first bias component vanishing under constant effects and the third vanishing under balanced allocation.

For $n\ge2$ with nonempty arms, standardized covariates and nonsingular arm fits under complete randomization, the two arm slopes decompose into population slopes and three errors, yielding the exact interacted bias expression and its first-component leverage-covariance formula.

Under the sequence assumptions stated in the caveats, eventual nonsingularity for every assignment and $\kappa_n\to0$, the noninteracted debiased estimator minus the average treatment effect equals the difference of arm means of the common-slope population residuals plus $o_p(n^{-1/2})$.

Under the sequence assumptions stated in the caveats, eventual armwise nonsingularity for every assignment and $\kappa_n\to0$, the interacted debiased estimator minus the average treatment effect equals the difference of arm means of the arm-specific population residuals plus $o_p(n^{-1/2})$.

overview.overview: The work studies the randomization bias of linear covariate adjustment and constructs exactly unbiased corrections for regressions with common slopes and with treatment-specific slopes. The Lean development covers finite-sample bias decompositions and unbiasedness, asymptotic linear expansions of the debiased estimators, and counterexamples and repairs concerning covariance bounds, bias signs and the one-covariate endpoint. Two selected repairs remain explicitly conditional on published sampling theorems.

text.body: The Lean statement formalizes the first example of P005-E002, in which $n=6$, the treatment arm has $n_T=4$ units, $a=(0,-3,-1,2,-4,-3)$ and $b=(2,1,3,-3,1,1)$. It asserts that there are 15 assignments, that $\bar a=-3/2$, $\bar b=5/6$ and $\overline{ab}-\bar a\bar b=-23/12$, and that $\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_T(a,b)$ has expectation $-69/40$ and variance $16607/4800$. It asserts further that the right-hand side of the printed bound equals $3829/1440$, which is smaller than the variance. Three supporting statements list the six units and the fifteen subsets of size four, and write the expectation as the average over these subsets. An assignment is represented by the set of treated units, and the randomization distribution is uniform on the subsets of size $n_T$. Expectations and variances are exact averages over all of these subsets. The statement contradicts the bound for vectors that are not centered. It does not contain the value $835/128$ of the centered bound, which the finding reports for the same example.

text.body: The main Lean statement is the corrected lemma of P005-E002. Let $n\ge4$ and $1\le n_T\le n-1$, let $t\in\{T,C\}$, and let $a$ and $b$ be arbitrary real vectors of length $n$, with $a_i^c=a_i-\bar a$ and $b_i^c=b_i-\bar b$. Assuming the quadratic-sampling result in Lemma A.5 of the supplement to Lei and Ding (2021), the main statement asserts the expectation identity as printed, and the bound $\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_t(a,b)\bigr)\le\frac{2(n-n_t)}{n_t(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(a_i^cb_i^c-\overline{a^cb^c}\bigr)^2+\frac{2(n-n_t)n}{n_t^3(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i^c)^2\times\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(b_i^c)^2 .$ Two supporting statements give steps of the proof on p. 1511. The first says that the covariance estimator of a nonempty arm is unchanged when a constant is subtracted from $a$ and another from $b$. The second is the inequality $\operatorname{Var}(U-V)\le2\operatorname{Var}U+2\operatorname{Var}V$ for two functions $U$ and $V$ of the assignment. The control arm is the complement of the treatment arm, and the variance is the exact average of squared deviations over all assignments. The lemma prints only $n\ge4$, and the Lean statement adds that both arms are nonempty, as in the setting of the paper. The moment calculation for the product of the two sample means, on which the derivation in the finding rests, is not stated separately.

text.body: The Lean statement formalizes the second example of P005-E002. In it $n=16$, $n_T=8$, the single covariate is $x=(8c,-8c,c,-c,\ldots,c,-c)$ with $c=\sqrt{8/71}$, and the outcomes are $y(1)=(1/64,1/64,1,\ldots,1)$ and $y(0)=0$. The statement asserts that the conditions of the paper hold at this $n$: $\bar x=0$ and $\overline{x^2}=1$, the mean square of $y(1)$ is at most $1$, that of $y(0)$ is $0$, and $1/4<n_T/n<3/4$. It asserts that $\widehat L$, $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ are invertible under each of the 12870 assignments, that $\kappa=32/71$, and that $h_iy_i(1)=8/71$ for every $i$. The variance of $\overline{hy(1)}_T-\bar h_T\overline{y(1)}_T$ is $1678565511/8259174400$. The first line of the display on p. 1517 equals $117645319/619438080$ and the second line equals $334349/1744896$, and both are smaller than the variance. The variance is the exact average over all 12870 treated sets, and the statement does not reduce it to the number of high-leverage units in the treatment arm. The statement concerns this one population. It includes neither the centered bound nor the repetition of the population that places it in a sequence satisfying Assumptions 1–3.

text.body: Two Lean statements give the corrected chain of P005-E002, for either arm $t$ with its outcome $y(t)$. The first is for a fixed $n\ge4$ with $1\le n_T\le n-1$, $\bar x=0$, $\overline{xx'}=I_d$ and $n^{-1}\sum_iy_i(t)^2\le K$. Let $u_i=h_i-d$ and $v_i=y_i(t)-\overline{y(t)}$. The statement asserts that $\bar h=d$, $0\le h_i\le n\kappa$, $|u_i|\le n\kappa$ and $d\le n\kappa$, and that $n^{-1}\sum_iu_i^2\le n\kappa d$, $n^{-1}\sum_iv_i^2\le K$ and $n^{-1}\sum_i(u_iv_i-\overline{uv})^2\le n^2\kappa^2K$. It then asserts that the variance of $\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_t(h,y(t))$ is at most the bound of the corrected Lemma A.1, and that this bound is at most $\frac{2(n-n_t)}{n_t(n-1)}n^2\kappa^2K+\frac{2(n-n_t)n}{n_t^3(n-1)}n\kappa dK .$ The second statement is for a sequence of populations satisfying Assumptions 1–3. It asserts that this variance is $O(\kappa^2n+\kappa d/n)$, and that the variance of $n^{-1}\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_t(h,y(t))$ is $O(\kappa^2/n+\kappa d/n^3)$. Eleven supporting statements give the elementary facts: the linearity and monotonicity of averages, the identity $\overline{(a-\bar a)^2}=\overline{a^2}-\bar a^2$, the bounds $0\le h_i\le n\kappa$, the identity $\bar h=d$ when $\overline{xx'}=I_d$, and the bounds on $u$ and $v$ listed above. In the sequence statement, $K$ and the bounds on $n_T/n$ are the same for every $n\ge3$, Assumption 2 holds for all large $n$, and $1\le d_n\le n$. The requirement $d_n\ge1$ excludes populations without covariates, which the paper does not discuss. The second statement bounds the variance itself, and the bounds on the two coefficients under Assumption 3 are not stated separately.

text.body: For $n\ge3$, index the units by $i=1,\ldots,n$ and set $v_1=0$ and $v_i=-1+2(i-2)/(n-2)$ for $i=2,\ldots,n$. Set $\epsilon=n^{-2}$, $a_1=1$, $a_i=\epsilon v_i$ for $i\ge2$, $q=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n(a_j-1/n)^2$ and $x_i=(a_i-1/n)/\sqrt q$. The main Lean statement concerns this sequence from P005-E001, with $d=1$, $n_T=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and $y_i(1)=y_i(0)=v_i$. It asserts that the sequence satisfies Assumptions 1–3. For every $n\ge6$ the covariate has mean $0$ and mean square $1$, both outcomes have mean square at most $1$, $1/4<n_T/n<3/4$, and $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ are invertible under every assignment. The statement asserts that $\kappa\to1$ while $\kappa\log d=0$, and that the average treatment effect is $0$. For every even $n\ge6$ and every assignment, it asserts that the remainder $R_n$ of the expansion satisfies $|R_n|\ge n-6$, and it concludes that $R_n$ is not $O_p(\sqrt{\kappa/n})$. A supporting statement says that $\kappa_n\log1=0$ for every sequence $\kappa_n$, so the printed condition holds at $d=1$ whatever the maximum leverage. Here $R_n=O_p(r_n)$ means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exist $M$ and $n_0$ such that $\Pr(|R_n|>Mr_n)<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge n_0$, where the probability is the fraction of assignments. The bounds of Assumptions 1 and 3 are asserted from $n=3$ on, while the finding begins at $n=6$. The closed form of $\kappa$ and the separate bounds on the estimator and on the linear term are not part of the statement.

text.body: The Lean statement is the corrected last paragraph of Theorem 4.1 given in P005-E001. It concerns a sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$, in which the number of covariates $d_n$, the covariates, the potential outcomes and $n_{T,n}$ may all change with $n$. Assumption 1 holds with one constant $K$ and Assumption 3 with one pair of constants for every $n\ge3$, and Assumption 2 holds for all large $n$. The matrices $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ are invertible under every assignment for all large $n$. Let $R_n=\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I-\mathrm{ATE}-\frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\bigl(y_i(1)-\overline{y(1)}-x_i'\beta_{I,T}\bigr)+\frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\bigl(y_i(0)-\overline{y(0)}-x_i'\beta_{I,C}\bigr).$ Assuming the row-sampling result in Lemma 3.4 of Tropp (2011), the statement asserts that if $\kappa_n\log\max\{d_n,2\}\to0$, then $R_n=O_p(\sqrt{\kappa_nd_n/n})$. This means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exist $M$ and $n_0$ such that $\Pr(|R_n|>M\sqrt{\kappa_nd_n/n})<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge n_0$, where the probability is the fraction of assignments at size $n$. The sequence begins at $n=3$ and has $1\le d_n\le n$. The estimator, the linear term and the order of the remainder are those printed; the leverage condition is $\kappa_n\log\max\{d_n,2\}\to0$.

text.body: The main Lean statement is the expansion of Theorem 4.1 under the condition $\kappa_n\log(2d_n)\to0$, which is the condition of the derivation in P005-N004. It concerns a sequence of finite populations with $1\le d_n\le n$ that satisfies Assumptions 1–3, with constants that do not depend on $n$, and in which $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ are invertible under every assignment for all large $n$. Assuming the row-sampling result in Lemma 3.4 of Tropp (2011), the main statement asserts that the remainder of the expansion is $O_p(\sqrt{\kappa_nd_n/n})$, as printed. Two supporting statements relate this condition to the condition $\kappa\log\max\{d,2\}=o(1)$ of P005-E001. The first asserts that $\log\max\{d,2\}\le\log(2d)\le2\log\max\{d,2\}$ for every integer $d\ge1$. The second concerns sequences such that $d_n\ge1$ and $\kappa_n\ge0$ for all large $n$. It asserts that $\kappa_n\log(2d_n)\to0$ if and only if $\kappa_n\log\max\{d_n,2\}\to0$, and that either condition implies $\kappa_n\to0$ and $\kappa_n\log d_n\to0$. It asserts further that if $d_n\ge2$ for all large $n$, then the printed condition $\kappa_n\log d_n\to0$ is equivalent to both.

text.body: The Lean statement formalizes the example of P005-E013, in which $n=6$, $n_T=2$, the single covariate is $x=\sqrt{3/20}\,(-3,-2,-1,0,1,5)$, and the outcomes are $y(1)=(9,4,1,0,1,25)$ and $y(0)=0$. It asserts that $\bar x=0$ and $\overline{x^2}=1$, that $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ are invertible under each of the 15 assignments, that $y(1)$ has mean square at most $121$, and that $1/4<n_T/n<3/4$. With the printed weight $1/8$, the expression $\overline{y(1)}_T-\bar x_T'\hat N_T+\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_T(h,y(1))/8$ has expectation $4913/1200$. With the weight $1/2$ derived two displays earlier, the expectation is $20/3$, which equals $\overline{y(1)}$. The statement concludes that the expression with the printed weight is not unbiased for $\overline{y(1)}$. This expression is the second line of the printed display after the inverse terms cancel, with the transposes of P005-E010 restored. Six supporting statements connect the rational arithmetic to the covariate with the factor $\sqrt{3/20}$. For one covariate $x=sa$ they give $h_i=s^2a_i^2$, $\bar x_T'\hat N_T=s^2\bar a_T\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_T(a,y)$ and $\det\widehat L_T=s^2\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_T(a,a)$, the scaling of a sample covariance, and Assumption 2 when $\bar a=0$ and $s^2\overline{a^2}=1$.

text.body: Four Lean statements cover the corrected display of P005-E013, with the transposes of P005-E010. The first is the algebra of the display for $n\ge3$, an arbitrary real weight $c$, and a nonempty arm such that $\widehat L_T$ is invertible. It asserts that the inverse terms cancel: the first line of the display, with $c$ in place of the weight, equals $\overline{y(1)}_T-\bar x_T'\hat N_T+c\,\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_T(h,y(1))=\overline{y(1)}_T-\bar x_T'N_T-\bar x_T'(\hat N_T-N_T)+c\,\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_T(h,y(1)).$ The second assumes $n\ge3$, $2\le n_T\le n-1$ and $\bar x=0$, and asserts that this expression has expectation $\overline{y(1)}+\Bigl(-\frac{n_C}{n_T(n-1)}+N_{\mathrm{TTT}}+c\,\frac{(n_T-1)n}{n_T(n-1)}\Bigr)S_1,\qquad S_1=\overline{hy(1)}-\bar h\,\overline{y(1)} .$ It asserts that the bracket vanishes exactly when $c=n_C/((n-2)n_T)$, and that the expression with this weight has expectation $\overline{y(1)}$. It also gives the bias that remains with the printed weight $n_T/((n-2)n_C)$. The third is the same statement for the control arm when $n_C\ge2$, with the weight $n_T/((n-2)n_C)$. The fourth is for a sequence of populations satisfying Assumptions 1–3 with $d_n\ge1$. It asserts for either arm $t$ that the debiased estimator of the arm minus $\overline{y(t)}_t-\bar x_t'N_t$ is $O_p(\sqrt{\kappa/n})$. Three supporting statements give the symmetry of the product $u'v$, the bound $h_i\le n$, and the interval $d/n\le\kappa\le1$ when $\overline{xx'}=I_d$. The fourth statement assumes neither $\kappa=o(1)$ nor invertibility, since the inverse has cancelled from the estimator.

text.body:
Four Lean statements cover the corrections of P005-E010 outside Appendix B.4. The first is the display on p. 1516 with the transpose restored and the control sum taken over $[C]$. For $n\ge3$ and every assignment under which $\widehat L$ is invertible, it asserts that $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{\mathrm{Debiased}}=\overline{y(1)}_T-\overline{y(0)}_C-( ar x_T- ar x_C)'\hat N+ rac{1}{n-2}\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_T(h,y(1))- rac{1}{n-2}\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_C(h,y(0)),$ and that for every vector $v$ it also equals $ rac1{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]} igl(y_i(1)-x_i'v igr)- rac1{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]} igl(y_i(0)-x_i'v igr)-( ar x_T- ar x_C)'(\hat N-v)$ plus the same two covariance terms. The printed display is the case $v=N$, so the Lean statement is broader in this respect. The second statement is the identity of p. 1515: if $ ar x=0$, then $ ar x_C- ar x_T= ar x_C/p_T=- ar x_T/p_C$ for every assignment. The third formalizes the sentence of Remark 2 that $( ar x_C- ar x_T)'
u_2$ contains no unknowns. It asserts that there exists a function of the assignment, the covariates and the observed outcomes, chosen before the population, that equals this term for every population satisfying Assumption 2. Two supporting statements say that $\overline{x'v}_S= ar x_S'v$ and that an average over an arm depends only on the values in that arm. The fourth statement gives the exact decomposition in Theorem 3.1, including the bias $\mathbb E[( ar x_C- ar x_T)'(
u_1+

text.body: The Lean statement gives the two coefficient identities of the passage corrected in P005-E009. Let $n_T\ge2$ and $n_C\ge2$ be integers, and let $n=n_T+n_C$. The statement asserts that $\frac{1}{n-1}\cdot\frac{n_C(n-1)}{(n_C-1)n}-N_{\mathrm{TTC}}\,\frac{n_T(n-1)}{(n_C-1)n}=\frac{1}{n-2},\qquad-\frac{1}{n-1}\cdot\frac{n_T(n-1)}{(n_T-1)n}+N_{\mathrm{TTT}}\,\frac{n_T^2(n-1)}{n_C(n_T-1)n}=-\frac{1}{n-2}.$ It asserts further that, for all real numbers $A$ and $B$, the combination of $A$ and $B$ with the coefficients of equations (11) and (12) equals $B/(n-2)-A/(n-2)$. With $A=\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_T(h,y(1))$ and $B=\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_C(h,y(0))$, this is line (7) of Theorem 3.2. The two sample covariances are replaced by arbitrary real numbers, so the statement is an identity between coefficients and is broader than the printed sentence. The correction replaces $\overline{hy(0)y(0)}_C$ by $\bar h_C\,\overline{y(0)}_C$ in the name of the term, and an identity between coefficients cannot express it. The intermediate fraction $(n-n_Tn)/((n-2)(n_T-1)n)$ of the printed display is omitted.

e j$, and that $\mathbb E[D_iD_jD_s]=n_T(n_T-1)(n_T-2)/(n(n-1)(n-2))$ for distinct $i$, $j$ and $s$. It asserts the two equalities of the proof, with the expectation inside the double sum and with every sum running to $n$: $\mathbb E\Bigl[\sum_{i=1}^nD_ix_iy_i\sum_{j
e i}D_jz_j\Bigr]=- rac{n_T(n_T-1)}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i=1}^nx_iy_iz_i,$ $\mathbb E\Bigl[\sum_{i=1}^nD_ix_i\sum_{j
e i}D_jy_j\sum_{s
otin\{i,j\}}D_sz_s\Bigr]= rac{2n_T(n_T-1)(n_T-2)}{n(n-1)(n-2)}\sum_{i=1}^nx_iy_iz_i .$ It then asserts the decomposition of $ ar x_T ar y_T ar z_T$ in the last display and both conclusions of the lemma, $\mathbb E[ ar x_T ar y_T ar z_T]=N_{\mathrm{TTT}}\,\overline{xyz}$ and $\mathbb E[ ar x_T ar y_T ar z_C]=N_{\mathrm{TTC}}\,\overline{xyz}$. Of the seven supporting statements, one simplifies the coefficient to $N_{\mathrm{TTT}}/n$. The others give the probability that every unit of a given set is treated, the value $\mathbb E[D_i]=n_T/n$, the linearity of the expectation, and the identity $\sum_iD_ia_i=\sum_{i\in[T]}a_i$. The vectors have scalar entries, as in the lemma, and $D_i$ indicates that unit $i$ belongs to the treatment arm. The statement includes the second equality of the lemma, for which the printed proof gives no details.

text.body: Three Lean statements cover the display with the index corrected as in P005-E007. Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ satisfy $\overline{xx'}=I_d$, let $\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n$ be arbitrary real numbers, and let $\mu=n^{-1}\sum_kx_k\delta_k$. The first statement is the identity quoted below the display, $\sum_{i,j}(x_i'x_ja_j)^2=n\sum_ja_j^2\|x_j\|_2^2$ for all real $a_1,\ldots,a_n$. The second assumes $n\ge2$ and $1\le n_T\le n-1$. It asserts that $\sum_j(x_i'(x_j\delta_j-\mu))^2\le\sum_j(x_i'x_j\delta_j)^2$ for each $i$, and that $\Bigl(\frac1{p_Cn_Tn}\Bigr)^2\frac{n_Tn_C}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i,j}(x_i'x_j\delta_j)^2=\Bigl(\frac1{p_Cn_Tn}\Bigr)^2n^2\frac{n_Tn_C}{n(n-1)}\sum_jn^{-1}\|x_j\|_2^2\delta_j^2 ,$ which is the corrected third line. It asserts further that this quantity equals $\overline{h\delta^2}/(p_Tp_Cn(n-1))$ and is at most $\kappa\,\overline{\delta^2}/(p_Tp_C(n-1))$. The third is for a sequence of populations satisfying Assumptions 1–3 with $0\le d_n\le n$ for every $n\ge3$, and it takes $\delta_j=e_j(1)-e_j(0)$, the difference of the residuals of p. 1513. It asserts that $\overline{h\delta^2}/(p_Tp_Cn(n-1))$ is $O(\kappa/n)$. Zero covariates are allowed, including sequences with both zero and positive dimensions. The sequence assumptions use one moment constant and one pair of allocation bounds for every $n\ge3$, and centered, normalized covariates for all sufficiently large $n$. Two supporting statements give $v'\,\overline{xa}=\overline{(v'x)a}$ and the bound $n^{-1}\sum_j(e_j(1)-e_j(0))^2\le4K$ under Assumption 1. The statements concern the right-hand side of the display, and they do not assert its first inequality, which bounds $\operatorname{Var}[(*)]$ by Lemma A.5 of Lei and Ding (2021). The first two statements hold for arbitrary $\delta$, which is more than the display needs.

text.body: Two Lean statements give the identity that the display asserts once the surplus parenthesis of P005-N005 is deleted. The first takes an assignment with $1\le n_T\le n-1$ and arbitrary real numbers $e_i(1)$ and $e_i(0)$ such that $p_T\sum_ix_ie_i(1)+p_C\sum_ix_ie_i(0)=0$. Let $\delta_i=e_i(1)-e_i(0)$, $A=n^{-1}\sum_ix_i\delta_i$, $B=n^{-1}\sum_ix_ie_i(0)$ and $U=n^{-1}\sum_{i\in[T]}x_i\delta_i$. The statement asserts that $B=-p_TA$ and that $U+B=\frac1n\sum_{i\in[T]}\Bigl(x_i\delta_i+\frac{1}{p_T}B\Bigr)=\frac1n\sum_{i\in[T]}\bigl(x_i\delta_i-A\bigr),$ so the three lines of the display agree after multiplication by $p_C^{-1}\bar x_T'$. The second statement takes the residuals of p. 1513 under Assumption 2. It asserts that $\bar x_T-\bar x_C=\bar x_T/p_C$, that the residuals satisfy the relation above, and that the term $(*)$ equals $p_C^{-1}\bar x_T'(U+B)$, the first line of the display. Seven supporting statements give the steps of the second statement, among them that $\overline{x(x'v)}=v$ when $\overline{xx'}=I_d$ and that $n^{-1}\sum_ix_ie_i(D_i)=U+B$. The Lean statements place the population average inside the sum over $[T]$, as the display does. A surplus parenthesis has no counterpart in a formal statement, so the statements express the corrected display and cannot express the misprint.

text.body: The Lean statement negates the universal conjunction in the printed lemma, quantified over $n\ge4$, $1\le n_T\le n-1$, $t\in\{T,C\}$ and arbitrary real vectors $a$ and $b$ of length $n$. The conjunction being negated consists of the expectation identity $\mathbb E\bigl[\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_t(a,b)\bigr]=\frac{(n_t-1)n}{n_t(n-1)}\bigl(\overline{ab}-\bar a\bar b\bigr)$ together with the variance bound whose right-hand side is computed from $a$ and $b$ themselves, without centering. The two parts form one statement, as in the lemma. The variance bound is the part that P005-E002 corrects, and the six-unit example of that finding contradicts it. The expectation identity is the same in the corrected lemma and is not separately negated. The Lean statement adds to the printed hypotheses only that both arms are nonempty.

text.body: Three Lean statements address the theorem as it is printed. The first holds the parts that need no correction: the decompositions of $\widehat\beta_{I,T}$ and $\widehat\beta_{I,C}$, the expression for the bias, and the first displayed identity. It is also the Lean statement for the exact part of the theorem that stands as printed. Its hypotheses are $n\ge2$, nonempty arms, standardization and invertibility of both arm matrices under every assignment. The second negates the universal identity in the last display on p. 1509 with the printed signs. Let $n\ge3$ and $1\le n_T\le n-1$, let $\bar x=0$ and $\overline{xx'}=I_d$, and let $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ be invertible under every assignment. The universal identity being negated is $E\bigl[\bar x_C'\nu_{3C}\bigr]-E\bigl[\bar x_T'\nu_{3T}\bigr]=N_{\mathrm{CCC}}S_0-N_{\mathrm{TTT}}S_1,\qquad S_t=\overline{hy(t)}-\bar h\,\overline{y(t)} .$ The third negates the universal expansion claim in the last paragraph of the theorem with the printed condition, for sequences of populations satisfying Assumptions 1–3 in which $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ are invertible under every assignment for all large $n$. The claim being negated says that if $\kappa_n\log d_n\to0$, then the remainder of the expansion is $O_p(\sqrt{\kappa_nd_n/n})$, and it admits $d_n=1$. The second and third statements negate the printed claims that P005-E003 and P005-E001 correct; the examples of those findings contradict the respective identity and expansion. The theorem is stated “Under Assumptions 1–3”. The two exact statements use Assumption 2 at the sample size considered and the invertibility of footnote 4, and not Assumptions 1 and 3.

text.body: The main Lean statement is the first part of the theorem at a fixed sample size. Let $n\ge3$ and $1\le n_T\le n-1$, let $\bar x=0$ and $\overline{xx'}=I_d$, and let $\widehat L$ be invertible under every assignment; the potential outcomes are arbitrary. The estimator $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}$ is the expression (3) with $\widehat\beta=\widehat L^{-1}\widehat N$, and $\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}$ is the expression (7)–(8). The statement asserts that $\mathbb E\bigl[\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}\bigr]=\mathbb E\bigl[\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}\bigr]-\mathrm{ATE},\qquad\mathbb E\bigl[\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{\mathrm{Debiased}}\bigr]=\mathrm{ATE},$ where the expectation is the average over all assignments of $n_T$ units to treatment. A supporting statement says that the mean of the treatment arm is unbiased for the population mean. The theorem prints only “Under Assumption 2”. The Lean statement adds $n\ge3$, which the factor $1/(n-2)$ requires, and the invertibility of footnote 4. The estimator is defined by the closed form (3), and the statement does not derive this form from the regression (1).

text.body: The main Lean statement is the first part of the theorem at a fixed sample size. Let $n\ge3$ and $1\le n_T\le n-1$, let $\bar x=0$ and $\overline{xx'}=I_d$, and let $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ be invertible under every assignment. The estimator $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I$ is the display of Section 4 with the slopes $\widehat\beta_{I,T}=\widehat L_T^{-1}\widehat N_T$ and $\widehat\beta_{I,C}=\widehat L_C^{-1}\widehat N_C$, and $\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}_I$ is as printed. The statement asserts that $\mathbb E[\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}_I]=\mathbb E[\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I]-\mathrm{ATE}$ and $\mathbb E[\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{I,\mathrm{Debiased}}]=\mathrm{ATE}$. It asserts further that each arm is unbiased separately: $\mathbb E\Bigl[\overline{y(1)}_T-\bar x_T'\widehat N_T+\frac{n_C}{(n-2)n_T}\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_T(h,y(1))\Bigr]=\overline{y(1)},$ and likewise for the control arm with the weight $n_T/((n-2)n_C)$. A supporting statement gives the algebra: for every assignment, $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{I,\mathrm{Debiased}}$ is the difference of these two expressions, in which no inverse appears. The theorem prints only “Under Assumption 2”, and the Lean statement adds $n\ge3$ and the invertibility of footnote 4. The slopes are those that Section 4 defines, in the reading of P005-E004, and the statement does not derive the estimator from the regression (2).

text.body: The Lean statement is the expansion for a sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$, in which the number of covariates $d_n$, the covariates, the potential outcomes and $n_{T,n}$ may all change with $n$. Assumption 1 holds with one constant $K$ and Assumption 3 with one pair of constants for every $n\ge3$, and Assumption 2 holds for all large $n$. The matrix $\widehat L$ is invertible under every assignment for all large $n$. Let $R_n=\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}-\mathrm{ATE}-\frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\bigl(y_i(1)-\overline{y(1)}-x_i'\beta^*\bigr)+\frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\bigl(y_i(0)-\overline{y(0)}-x_i'\beta^*\bigr).$ The statement asserts that if $d_n/n\to0$, then $R_n=O_p(\sqrt{\kappa_nd_n/n})$. Here $R_n=O_p(r_n)$ means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exist $M$ and $n_0$ such that $\Pr(|R_n|>Mr_n)<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge n_0$, where the probability is the fraction of assignments at size $n$. The statement requires $1\le d_n\le n$, and so it excludes populations without covariates, which the paper does not discuss. The condition and the order of the remainder are those printed.

text.body: The Lean statement is the expansion for a sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$, in which $d_n$, the covariates, the potential outcomes and $n_{T,n}$ may all change with $n$. Assumptions 1 and 3 hold with constants that do not depend on $n$, Assumption 2 holds for all large $n$, and $\widehat L$ is invertible under every assignment for all large $n$. The statement asserts that if $\kappa_n\to0$, then $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{\mathrm{Debiased}}-\mathrm{ATE}-\frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\bigl(y_i(1)-\overline{y(1)}-x_i'\beta^*\bigr)+\frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\bigl(y_i(0)-\overline{y(0)}-x_i'\beta^*\bigr)=o_p\bigl(n^{-1/2}\bigr).$ Here $R_n=o_p(r_n)$ means that $\Pr(|R_n|>\delta r_n)\to0$ for every $\delta>0$, where the probability is the fraction of assignments at size $n$. The statement requires $1\le d_n\le n$. It is the theorem as printed, and it does not include the bound $O_p(\sqrt{\kappa/n})$ that the proof in Appendix B.2 obtains without the condition $\kappa=o(1)$. That proof uses the variance bound of Lemma A.1, which P005-E002 corrects, and the correction does not change the theorem.

text.body: The Lean statement is the expansion for a sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$, in which $d_n$, the covariates, the potential outcomes and $n_{T,n}$ may all change with $n$. Assumptions 1 and 3 hold with constants that do not depend on $n$, Assumption 2 holds for all large $n$, and $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ are invertible under every assignment for all large $n$. The statement asserts that if $\kappa_n\to0$, then $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{I,\mathrm{Debiased}}-\bigl(\overline{y(1)}-\overline{y(0)}\bigr)-\frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\bigl(y_i(1)-\overline{y(1)}-x_i'\beta_{I,T}\bigr)+\frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\bigl(y_i(0)-\overline{y(0)}-x_i'\beta_{I,C}\bigr)=o_p\bigl(n^{-1/2}\bigr).$ Here $R_n=o_p(r_n)$ means that $\Pr(|R_n|>\delta r_n)\to0$ for every $\delta>0$, where the probability is the fraction of assignments at size $n$. The estimator is $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I-\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}_I$ with the weights printed in the theorem, and $\beta_{I,T}=\overline{y(1)x}$ and $\beta_{I,C}=\overline{y(0)x}$. The statement requires $1\le d_n\le n$, and it does not include the bound $O_p(\sqrt{\kappa/n})$ for each arm that the proof in Appendix B.4 obtains. Since the theorem assumes $\kappa=o(1)$, the sequence with one covariate of P005-E001 does not satisfy its hypotheses.
